BBC News — published 2026-09-29T19:58:58Z, confirmed from article metadata. Search highlights.
"Will reforming the triple lock pay for social care reform?"
From April 2030 the pension would rise only by the highest of inflation or 2.5%. Burnham added it "will hold its value relative to earnings over time". "We are still awaiting full details from the government."
IFS: new system would raise the state pension by whichever is highest of inflation, 2.5%, or average earnings over time rather than every year. "The removal of this permanent ratchet is to be welcomed and marks a substantial step towards a more sustainable and predictable state pension system."
IFS estimates the present triple lock will increase annual state pension expenditure by £16bn a year by 2026-27 compared with earnings-linked uprating since 2011; had the new lock been in place instead, spending would be £9bn a year lower than currently.
OBR: analysed shifting to an earnings-linked state pension in 2030 vs keeping the triple lock — identified no significant savings until 2034; by 2040 annual saving estimated at 0.2% of GDP, equivalent to £6bn a year in today's money.
DOWNING STREET: has said the planned change will save £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s, "but did not provide detail on how it reached that figure."
Health Foundation: a lifetime care cost cap of c.£86,000 in England (Dilnot, 2011) would cost c.£4bn a year; a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would cost c.£18.5bn a year extra by 2036.
Government has clarified that an individual's direct care costs would be covered but accommodation costs in a residential or nursing home would not.
JONATHAN CRIBB (IFS): the pension reform "will not be the answer to funding universal social care".
